strengths: Simple, elegant, and practically appealing idea: replacing the standard target computation with the minimum between the online and target network predictions introduces virtually no additional hyperparameters and negligible computational overhead.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple RL paradigms and architectures: online discrete RL (DQN, IMPALA with LayerNorm, IQN), offline discrete RL (CQL), and continuous control (SAC with SimbaV1 and SimbaV2 across MuJoCo, HumanoidBench, and DMC-Hard).

Thorough ablation on operator choices (Figure 1 and Figures 19-20), comparing Min against Max, Mean, Random, Online-only, and Target-only, which convincingly validates that the minimum operator specifically provides the desired stabilizing and regularizing effect.
Clear comparisons against relevant related baselines designed to reduce overestimation or leverage online networks (Double DQN, FR-DQN, ScDQN, and Maxmin DQN).
Sound theoretical grounding showing that MINTO falls within the Generalized Q-learning framework of Lan et al. (2020), ensuring convergence in the tabular setting.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: The core algorithmic change is very simple and conceptually closely related to existing target clipping and ensemble minimization techniques (such as Lan et al., 2020 and Fujimoto et al., 2018), differing primarily by pairing the target network with the current online network rather than a separate ensemble member.

Restricted Atari evaluation: Experiments are conducted on a 15-game subset rather than the full 57-game Atari benchmark (or a standardized sample-efficient benchmark like Atari 100k), which leaves open whether the gains hold uniformly across the entire suite.

Comparison in continuous control / SAC: The paper primarily applies MINTO to a single-critic variant of SAC (inspired by Simba architectures). Standard SAC relies on clipped double Q-learning (twin critics). While the authors mention testing twin critics in Appendix B and observing conservative updates, it would be valuable to see direct head-to-head comparisons against standard twin-critic SAC across all continuous control tasks.

Lack of analysis regarding target update frequency / polyak coefficient: Since MINTO aims to mitigate the delay caused by slow target updates, it remains unclear how sensitive MINTO is to the target update interval $T$ (or $	au$), and whether tuning $T$ in standard DQN/CQL could recover a similar speedup.

strengths: Simple, elegant, and practical mechanism: Computing the bootstrap target via the minimum of the online network and target network estimates (MINTO) requires no new hyperparameters and adds negligible computational overhead (just an extra forward pass on next states).

Broad empirical evaluation: The authors evaluate MINTO across a wide spectrum of RL settings, including value-based discrete online RL (DQN, IQN), offline RL (CQL), and continuous control actor-critic methods (SAC with SimbaV1 and SimbaV2 architectures across MuJoCo, HumanoidBench, and DMC-Hard).

Consistent and noticeable empirical gains: MINTO shows solid improvements across many benchmarks, especially in offline RL (CQL) and discrete control (DQN and IQN), demonstrating both accelerated learning and higher asymptotic performance.

Comprehensive ablations and baselines: The ablation study comparing Min to Max, Mean, Random, Online-only, and Target-only clearly substantiates the design choice of the minimum operator. Comparisons with Double DQN, Maxmin DQN, FR-DQN, and ScDQN provide good positioning within related literature.

Good reproducibility: The submission includes exact pseudocode for all adapted algorithms, a concise JAX code snippet, complete hyperparameter tables, and per-environment learning curves in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual and theoretical novelty: Mechanistically, the idea is an incremental variation of existing estimation-bias reduction techniques such as Maxmin Q-learning and Double Q-learning. The theoretical convergence result (Corollary 1) is a straightforward application of the non-expansion framework from Lan et al. (2020) to tabular Q-learning.

Mixed results in continuous control: While improvements are clear on MuJoCo and HumanoidBench, performance on DMC-Hard is either roughly neutral (SimbaV1) or slightly degraded (SimbaV2), indicating that the minimum operator can induce underestimation or over-conservatism in certain task domains.

Reliance on a single-critic SAC formulation: In continuous control, MINTO is integrated into a single-critic SAC setup (following Simba). The authors note in Appendix B that applying MINTO across twin critics (resulting in a min over 4 estimates) leads to overly conservative updates. A more detailed empirical or theoretical discussion on how to harmoniously blend MINTO with multi-critic architectures in continuous control would strengthen the paper.

Evaluation on a subset of Atari: Experiments are performed on a 15-game subset rather than the complete 57-game Atari benchmark (though the Graesser et al. 2022 subset is a reasonable and recognized protocol for compute-constrained settings).

strengths: Simplicity and ease of integration: The proposed MINTO method modifies only the temporal-difference target calculation by taking the minimum of the online and target networks, requiring just a single additional forward pass and minimal lines of code.

Broad empirical scope: The paper tests the method across multiple reinforcement learning paradigms, including online discrete RL (DQN, IQN on Atari), offline discrete RL (CQL on Atari), and continuous control (SAC with Simba architectures on MuJoCo, HumanoidBench, and DMC-Hard).

Comprehensive operator ablation: The ablation comparing Min against Max, Mean, Random, Online-only, and Target-only provides clear empirical justification that the minimum operator is specifically responsible for the observed stability and performance improvements.
Adherence to statistical rigor: The evaluation follows best practices in deep RL reporting, using Interquartile Mean (IQM) with confidence intervals across multiple seeds.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual and algorithmic novelty: Combining estimates via a minimum operator is well-established in RL (e.g., Clipped Double Q-learning in TD3/SAC, Maxmin Q-learning). Applying the minimum between the online network and its lagged target network is a relatively incremental heuristic tweak rather than a conceptual breakthrough.

Absence of direct value estimation analysis: The paper claims to mitigate overestimation bias while preserving stability, but does not provide direct empirical measurements of value bias (e.g., comparing learned Q-values against ground-truth Monte Carlo rollouts). It remains unclear whether the method accurately estimates returns or achieves gains merely by inducing strong underestimation pessimism.

Incompatibility with standard twin-critic architectures: As acknowledged in Appendix B, extending MINTO to standard twin-critic setups (such as standard SAC or TD3) causes excessive conservatism and degrades performance. The method relies on single-critic architectures (Simba), limiting its plug-and-play usability in standard continuous control baselines without modifying critic design.

Evaluation on a restricted Atari benchmark: The online and offline Atari evaluations are conducted on only 14–15 selected games rather than the standard 57-game ALE suite. While these games represent different score profiles, a broader evaluation is necessary to confirm that the minimum operator does not hurt performance in exploration-demanding or reward-sparse tasks.

Trivial theoretical contribution: Corollary 1 and its proof in Appendix A are straightforward verifications of non-expansion properties that directly follow from the Generalized Q-learning framework of Lan et al. (2020), offering limited new theoretical insight into deep RL dynamics.

strengths: Simple, elegant, and practical method: MINTO is straightforward to implement, introduces no new hyperparameters, and adds minimal computational overhead (just an additional forward evaluation of the online network).

Extensive empirical coverage across multiple RL paradigms: The paper demonstrates benefits across online discrete control (DQN, IQN on Atari), offline RL (CQL on Atari), and online continuous control (SAC with SimbaV1, SimbaV2, and CrossQ+WN on MuJoCo, HumanoidBench, and DMC-Hard).

Insightful analysis and ablations: The comparison among different operators (Min, Max, Mean, Random, Online-only, Target-only in Section 4.2), the tracking of the online selection ratio over training, and the value estimation error/bias analysis on Car-on-the-Hill provide solid intuition for why the minimum operator succeeds.
Well-structured presentation and commitment to reproducibility, including detailed pseudocode for each integrated algorithm, explicit hyperparameter tables, and code availability.
weaknesses: Incremental conceptual novelty: The core idea of taking the minimum across value estimates to combat overestimation bias is well established in deep RL (e.g., Clipped Double Q-learning in TD3/SAC, Maxmin Q-learning). While applying it between the target and online network is effective and practical, the methodological novelty is relatively modest.

Evaluation on a subset of Atari: Experiments are performed on a 15-game subset recommended by Graesser et al. (2022). While this subset covers a spread of difficulties, evaluating across the standard 57 or 26 Atari-50M games would provide a more comprehensive validation for a core value-learning modification.

Theoretical analysis is an immediate corollary of existing work: The convergence result directly invokes the Generalized Q-learning framework of Lan et al. (2020) in the tabular setting, which guarantees convergence for any non-expansion target operator. It does not explain the practical interaction between deep function approximation, moving targets, and the online-target minimum.

Mixed gains in continuous control: In continuous control benchmarks such as DMC-Hard, MINTO yields comparable or slightly inferior results compared to the baselines (e.g., SimbaV2 in Fig. 7 and Fig. 22). Furthermore, when Polyak averaging (soft updates) is used rather than periodic hard updates, $Q_\theta$ and $Q_{\bar{\theta}}$ tend to remain very close, which warrants a deeper investigation into how the update rate $\tau$ interacts with the online-target minimum.

strengths: Simplicity and ease of adoption: MINTO proposes an exceptionally simple modification to the TD target computation—taking the minimum between the target network and online network predictions—which requires only minimal code changes, adds negligible computational overhead, and introduces no new hyperparameters.

Broad and thorough empirical validation: The method is comprehensively evaluated across discrete and continuous action spaces, online and offline paradigms (DQN, IQN, CQL, SAC/Simba, CrossQ+WN), and multiple network architectures (standard CNN, IMPALA with LayerNorm, SimbaV1/V2).

Principled operator ablation: Section 4.2 and Appendix D.7 provide a well-designed empirical comparison among different operators (Min, Max, Mean, Random, Target-Only, Online-Only), demonstrating that the minimum operator specifically provides the desired balance between freshness and stability.

Solid empirical analysis of bias: The Car-on-the-Hill experiment in Appendix E provides clear insight into how MINTO mitigates overestimation bias without suffering from the excessive underestimation characteristic of multi-estimator approaches like Maxmin Q-learning.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual and theoretical novelty: Taking the minimum between value estimators to control overestimation is a well-established concept in deep RL (e.g., Clipped Double Q-learning, Maxmin Q-learning). Applying this between the online and target network is an intuitive heuristic, and the theoretical result (Corollary 1) is a straightforward application of the generalized Q-learning convergence framework from Lan et al. (2020) restricted to tabular MDPs.

Evaluation on a subset of Atari games: Experiments are conducted on a 15-game subset of the Arcade Learning Environment rather than the standard 57-game benchmark. While the 15-game subset is grounded in prior literature (Graesser et al., 2022), evaluating the full suite would provide stronger evidence against selection bias.

Mixed results in continuous control: On the DMC-Hard benchmark (Figure 7 and Figures 22-23), MINTO does not show meaningful improvement over the Simba baselines and in fact slightly degrades performance on SimbaV2, indicating that the conservative min operator may be sub-optimal in certain deterministic or low-noise environments.

strengths: Simplicity and ease of implementation: MINTO introduces a remarkably simple modification to the Bellman target calculation—taking the minimum between the online network and the target network—requiring only a single line of code and negligible computational overhead without introducing new hyperparameters.

Extensive and diverse empirical evaluation: The proposed method is thoroughly benchmarked across diverse domains, including discrete online RL (Atari with CNN and IMPALA architectures), distributional RL (IQN), offline RL (CQL), and continuous control (SimbaV1, SimbaV2, and CrossQ+WN on MuJoCo, HumanoidBench, and DMC-Hard).

Rigorous experimental methodology: The paper follows modern benchmarking standards, reporting Interquartile Mean (IQM) scores with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals across multiple seeds (5 to 10 seeds per task).

Comprehensive operator ablation and bias analysis: The ablation comparing alternative operators (Min, Max, Mean, Random, Online Only, Target Only) in Section 4.2 and the bias/MSE estimation analysis on Car-on-the-Hill in Appendix E provide clear empirical justification for why the minimum operator prevents runaway overestimation while still accelerating learning.

Meaningful comparisons against relevant baselines: The paper explicitly compares MINTO against closely related methods that modify bootstrapping or combat overestimation, including Double DQN, Maxmin DQN, Functional Regularization DQN (FR-DQN), and Self-correcting DQN (ScDQN).
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: While practically appealing and well-motivated, combining two Q-value estimates via a minimum operator is conceptually very close to Clipped Double Q-learning (TD3/SAC) and Maxmin Q-learning. Applying the min-operator between the online network and its lagged target network is a relatively straightforward heuristic.

Evaluation scope and benchmarks: The discrete control experiments are restricted to a 15-game subset of the Atari 2600 benchmark rather than the full 57-game suite. Furthermore, for offline RL, evaluation is limited to discrete Atari CQL datasets (RL Unplugged) without testing on standard continuous offline benchmarks such as D4RL.

Limited gains and mixed performance in continuous control: In the continuous control benchmarks (Section 5.4 and Figure 7), while MINTO improves sample efficiency on HumanoidBench and MuJoCo, the gains on DMC-Hard are marginal or slightly degraded (e.g., SimbaV2 on DMC-Hard). Additionally, standard continuous control actor-critic algorithms typically already maintain two critics (Clipped Double Q); incorporating MINTO when two critics are already present is less natural and yields smaller relative improvements.

Superficial theoretical contribution: Corollary 1 directly casts MINTO into the Generalized Q-learning framework of Lan et al. (2020) by simply re-stating that max and min are non-expansions. This does not capture the practical dynamics of neural network function approximation or moving target network intervals in deep RL.
